_comment: The crop and pan contract shared by crop_to_fill in
postroll/media/generate_collage.py and CollageGeometry.placement in
PostRollApp/Sources/Services/CollageGeometry.swift (#168). The geometry
is implemented twice, in two languages, and nothing but this file forces
the two to agree. When they disagree Dan sees one framing in the editor
and gets another in the exported file, which makes the preview a liar.
The rule:
photo_ratio = photo_w / photo_h, cell_ratio = cell_w / cell_h
fill_scale  = cell_h / photo_h  when photo_ratio > cell_ratio,
cell_w / photo_w  otherwise
effective   = fill_scale * max(zoom, zoom_floor)
rendered    = photo dimensions * effective
overflow    = rendered - cell, per axis
draw offset = -overflow * (0.5 + offset * 0.5)   where overflow > 0
(cell - rendered) / 2              where the photo has slack
draw_x and draw_y are the rendered photo's top-left corner relative to
the cell's top-left, so they are Swift's `committed` size directly and
the negation of Python's crop rect origin.
An offset only chooses which slice of an overflowing photo is kept. On an
axis where the photo is SMALLER than its cell there is nothing to discard,
so it is centred no matter what the offset says. The editor enforces this
already by refusing to commit a pan on an axis without overflow.
These numbers are computed from the rule above, never recorded from
either implementation, so a side that disagrees fails rather than
redefining the contract to match itself.
_tolerance_comment: Python truncates its pixel geometry with int() while Swift keeps CGFloat, so the two can land one pixel apart on the same case. A tolerance of 1px absorbs that and still catches every real drift: the 0.4-vs-0.5 vertical bias bug this file exists to prevent moved the crop by tens of pixels.
